{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"We are told that a shift changed at short notice is an inconvenience, a rotten surprise in an otherwise orderly system. That description is too small. When software changes your shift after you have arranged your day, it changes your power over the day. You lose the ability to trade hours with a coworker, plan childcare, take a second job, attend an appointment, or simply sleep without watching the phone. It’s a schedule that reaches through the locked door of your home.

The important fact is more than the short notice. It is that the decision arrives as weather: impersonal, automated, and apparently beyond appeal. A manager can say the application “generated” the change, while the application has an office, a conscience, and nobody who can be made to answer for the result. That’s useful bullshit. A rule written by people still governs the machine (even when the screen makes it look like fate), and that distinction matters.

Picture a kitchen where someone else moves the stove every time you reach for a pan. You can still cook, technically. You can still be blamed if dinner is late. But your effort now includes the constant work of finding the floor. Software scheduling does this to labour – it turns time itself into a variable controlled elsewhere, then treats your failure to absorb the variable as a personal defect.

Of course, a workplace may need to respond to a sick employee, a broken machine, or a genuine rush (rather than a permanent staffing plan). I accept the existence of changing conditions. The quarrel is with a system that makes workers carry every uncertainty while the institution keeps the power to demand certainty from them. If the business needs flexibility, it should pay for flexibility; that is the first honest translation of the problem.

What happens when a schedule is a promise only for the person receiving it, but a suggestion for the company issuing it? The answer is visible in the arithmetic. You reserve a bus, lose wages from a cancelled shift, arrive for work, or turn down another commitment, and each choice becomes a risk you bear alone. The software may display a neat calendar, yet the life behind it is being governed by a series of unstable permissions.

I mean “control” in a practical sense. Control is the ability to decide what you will do with your time and to make other plans without begging an opaque system for mercy – the ability to refuse a demand without converting refusal into hunger. A short-notice change removes that ability. It doesn’t need a guard at the door. It works by making refusal expensive, then calling the expense your lack of commitment.

We should be precise about the remedy. Workers need advance notice, a premium for late changes, a right to decline without retaliation, and a human route for correcting errors. Those terms belong in a contract or a collectively enforced rule, rather than in a cheerful promise that the app will improve. You’re not asking for the weather to stop changing; you’re asking the person who controls the roof to stop pretending the rain is your fault.

The screen offers options (on a screen), so everyone should be grateful. I think that argument confuses options with leverage. You may technically choose, but the choice is shaped by rent, food, transport, and the threat of losing future hours. That’s why we need to name unpredictability as a labour issue. We’re not describing a bad user experience. We’re describing a transfer of risk from the employer to the worker, and our bargaining power begins when that transfer becomes visible.

The practical work follows – compare the promised schedule with the changes, keep the messages, record the costs, and ask coworkers to do the same. The record becomes evidence when the pattern is written down. Then bring it to a union meeting, a workplace committee, or a collective conversation about what the schedule owes the people whose bodies make the business run. I want the demand to be plain: a schedule is part of the job, and changing it has a price. We can build that price into the rules. We are told that a shift changed at short notice is an inconvenience, a rotten surprise in an otherwise orderly system. That description is too small. When software changes your shift after you have arranged your day, it changes your power over the day. You lose the ability to trade hours with a coworker, plan childcare, take a second job, attend an appointment, or simply sleep without watching the phone. It’s a schedule that reaches through the locked door of your home.

The important fact is more than the short notice. It is that the decision arrives as weather: impersonal, automated, and apparently beyond appeal. A manager can say the application “generated” the change, while the application has an office, a conscience, and nobody who can be made to answer for the result. That’s useful bullshit. A rule written by people still governs the machine (even when the screen makes it look like fate), and that distinction matters.

Picture a kitchen where someone else moves the stove every time you reach for a pan. You can still cook, technically. You can still be blamed if dinner is late. But your effort now includes the constant work of finding the floor. Software scheduling does this to labour – it turns time itself into a variable controlled elsewhere, then treats your failure to absorb the variable as a personal defect.

Of course, a workplace may need to respond to a sick employee, a broken machine, or a genuine rush (rather than a permanent staffing plan). I accept the existence of changing conditions. The quarrel is with a system that makes workers carry every uncertainty while the institution keeps the power to demand certainty from them. If the business needs flexibility, it should pay for flexibility; that is the first honest translation of the problem.

What happens when a schedule is a promise only for the person receiving it, but a suggestion for the company issuing it? The answer is visible in the arithmetic. You reserve a bus, lose wages from a cancelled shift, arrive for work, or turn down another commitment, and each choice becomes a risk you bear alone. The software may display a neat calendar, yet the life behind it is being governed by a series of unstable permissions.

I mean “control” in a practical sense. Control is the ability to decide what you will do with your time and to make other plans without begging an opaque system for mercy – the ability to refuse a demand without converting refusal into hunger. A short-notice change removes that ability. It doesn’t need a guard at the door. It works by making refusal expensive, then calling the expense your lack of commitment.

We should be precise about the remedy. Workers need advance notice, a premium for late changes, a right to decline without retaliation, and a human route for correcting errors. Those terms belong in a contract or a collectively enforced rule, rather than in a cheerful promise that the app will improve. You’re not asking for the weather to stop changing; you’re asking the person who controls the roof to stop pretending the rain is your fault.

The screen offers options (on a screen), so everyone should be grateful. I think that argument confuses options with leverage. You may technically choose, but the choice is shaped by rent, food, transport, and the threat of losing future hours. That’s why we need to name unpredictability as a labour issue. We’re not describing a bad user experience. We’re describing a transfer of risk from the employer to the worker, and our bargaining power begins when that transfer becomes visible.

The practical work follows – compare the promised schedule with the changes, keep the messages, record the costs, and ask coworkers to do the same. The record becomes evidence when the pattern is written down. Then bring it to a union meeting, a workplace committee, or a collective conversation about what the schedule owes the people whose bodies make the business run. I want the demand to be plain: a schedule is part of the job, and changing it has a price. We can build that price into the rules. Otherwise the phone keeps ringing, and the kitchen keeps moving.
